title: Faith has six parts
hook: belief in Allah, His angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, and decree (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, fiqh close: the end of the long block on law. Your line was many roads, one direction. Did you catch someone doing a thing differently, and still facing the same way? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

The companions are sitting with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when a man walks in. His clothes are brilliantly white. His hair is very black. There's no dust of travel on him, and nobody in the room knows who he is. He sits down knee to knee with the Prophet, rests his hands on his own thighs, and starts asking questions. What is islam? The Prophet answers. The stranger says, you have spoken truly. The companions, as Umar tells it, were amazed that he asked and then confirmed the answer himself. Then the second question, the one that opens a new block of this path: tell me about iman.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `TELL ME ABOUT IMAN.`

segments.voice: This scene is in Sahih Muslim, and the answer to that second question is a list. Iman, the Prophet says, is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and to believe in the decree, its good and its harm. Six. The next week of this path takes them one at a time. First, notice the shape of the conversation. The stranger asks three things in order: islam, then iman, then ihsan. Islam is answered with things you do: the testimony, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage. Iman is answered with things you hold to be true. Ihsan is answered with the way you worship: as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, knowing that He sees you. So in one sitting the religion is laid out in layers: the body, the belief, and the heart. Second, the list didn't appear from nowhere. Much of it is already in the Qur'an. Pickthall's translation of one verse says of the believers: "Each one believeth in Allah and His angels and His scriptures and His messengers." The hadith gathers that together and adds the Last Day and the decree. Third, who the stranger was. After he leaves, the Prophet tells Umar it was Jibril, the angel Gabriel, who had come to teach the people their religion. An angel taught the list of beliefs that includes the angels. Last, why a list matters. Six short items are easy to carry. A child can count them on one hand and one more finger. A scholar can spend a life on any one of them.
screen: `ISLAM, IMAN, IHSAN.` · `THE LIST IS IN THE QUR'AN TOO.` · `THE STRANGER WAS JIBRIL.` · then, large: `SIX TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: The practice: say the six. Hold up one hand, and let your breathing slow. Fold a finger down for each one, slowly, and say it, aloud or in your head. Allah. The angels. The books. The messengers. The Last Day. Then the thumb of the other hand: the decree. Go through them a second time, slower, and notice which one you'd most like to understand better. You don't have to answer why. Just notice where your mind lingers. The bell holds the time.
Iman. Faith, belief: in the hadith of Jibril, belief in Allah, His angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Today's word.
Your line: six to believe. Today, count them once more on your fingers, somewhere unexpected: in a queue, at a red light. Tomorrow, the first of the six. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: The six articles of faith are taught as a list, and the hadith of Jibril is taught as a summary of the religion in three layers: islam, iman and ihsan.
